Designing a Nearby Service (Yelp / Google Maps Places)

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Intermediate Topics: Geohash, Quadtree, Spatial Indexing, Location Updates, Radius Queries Asked at: Google, Uber, Amazon, Swiggy, Zomato, PhonePe, Grab Prerequisites:Caching, Database Indexing, and Scalability

1. Understanding the Problem

A proximity service answers the question “what’s near me?” — restaurants within 2km, friends within 500m, EV chargers within 5km. The core challenge: indexing millions of locations (some static like restaurants, some moving like drivers) so that a radius query returns results in under 100ms without scanning the entire dataset. Bonus: efficiently updating the index when entities move.

Real examples: Yelp, Google Maps “Explore Nearby,” Uber driver matching, Swiggy restaurant discovery, Bumble/Hinge proximity matching.

2. Naive First Cut

Store all places with lat/lng. For each query, compute haversine distance to every row and filter.💡 Haversine is the formula for the distance between two points on a sphere - the correct way to measure “how far apart” on a globe. It involves trigonometry, which matters later because no database index can evaluate it.

Why this breaks:

  • Computing distance to every row in a table of 200M places is a full table scan
  • B-tree index on lat or lng alone doesn’t help (you need 2D range)💡 A B-tree is the ordinary database index: a sorted structure that is superb at “values between X and Y” in one dimension. Proximity is two dimensions at once, and that mismatch is the central problem of this whole design. Learn more →
  • Can’t scale to 100K QPS each doing a full scan💡 QPS = queries per second. A full table scan might be tolerable once; 100,000 times a second it is not, which is why the fix has to be a different index rather than a bigger machine. Learn more →
  • No support for moving entities (drivers, friends) that update every 5 seconds
  • Radius “2km” varies by latitude (longitude degree spacing shrinks at poles)
  • No ranking within results (closest first, highest rated first)

The rest of the doc evolves this into a geospatial index with Geohash-based sharding and efficient range queries.💡 A geospatial index is a structure built specifically for “what is near this point” rather than “what equals this value”. The trick they all share is turning two coordinates into one sortable key so an ordinary sorted index can answer a map question. Learn more →

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Uber H3 Hexagonal Grid - Uses a hierarchical hexagonal grid system (H3) to partition the earth into cells at multiple resolutions. Each hexagon has roughly equal area (unlike Geohash rectangles which distort at poles). Used for surge pricing, supply/demand balancing, and driver matching. (Uber Engineering)
  • Google S2 Geometry Library - Hierarchical decomposition of the sphere into cells using a Hilbert curve. Enables efficient spatial indexing where a region query becomes a set of contiguous cell range scans. Used in Google Maps and Pokémon Go. (S2 Geometry)
  • Redis Geo Commands - Redis GEOADD/GEOSEARCH uses a sorted set with Geohash-encoded scores. O(N+log(M)) for radius queries where N = results and M = total entries. Simple, fast, but single-machine memory-limited. (Redis Docs)
  • Foursquare Pilgrim SDK - Background location tracking with adaptive precision: high-frequency GPS in cities, low-frequency cell-tower in rural areas. Balances battery life vs accuracy for proximity features.

4. Functional Requirements

Core (Top 3)

  1. Find nearby places within a radius - given user’s location and a radius, return relevant places sorted by distance/rating
  2. Update location for moving entities - accept GPS pings from millions of devices every few seconds and keep the spatial index fresh
  3. Search with filters - combine proximity with attributes (cuisine type, price range, open now, rating > 4.0)

Below the Line

  • Place details, reviews, and photos
  • Route/ETA to each result
  • Saved/favorited places
  • Business owner place management
  • Check-ins and visit history

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core

  • Query latency: P99 < 100ms for radius queries💡 P99 = the figure 99% of queries stay under, so it is a promise about the unluckiest 1 in 100 rather than the average. Learn more →
  • Update throughput: Handle 2M+ location updates per second (for dynamic entities like drivers)
  • Freshness: Moving entity locations reflected in queries within 3-5 seconds of the update
  • Scale: 200M static places indexed; 10M concurrent moving entities

Below the Line

  • Multi-region serving (query the nearest data center)
  • Graceful degradation (return cached stale results if spatial index is slow)
  • Battery-aware SDK (reduce GPS polling frequency based on movement speed)

6. Core Entities

  • Place - a static location with metadata (restaurant, ATM, gas station) — lat, lng, category, rating, opening hours
  • MovingEntity - a dynamic location (driver, delivery partner, friend) — lat, lng, updated_at, entity_type
  • NearbyQuery - a request with center point, radius, filters, and sort preference
  • LocationUpdate - a GPS ping with entity_id, lat, lng, timestamp, accuracy

7. API / System Interface

GET /v1/nearby/places?lat=12.97&lng=77.59&radius=2000&category=restaurant&sort=distance&limit=20
Authorization: Bearer <token>

Response:
{
  "places": [
    {"id": "p1", "name": "Toit Brewpub", "distance_m": 340, "rating": 4.5, "lat": 12.972, "lng": 77.594},
    ...
  ]
}

POST /v1/location/update (from mobile SDK)
Body: {"entity_id": "driver_123", "lat": 12.971, "lng": 77.592, "timestamp": 1720000000, "accuracy_m": 8}
Response: 202 Accepted

GET /v1/nearby/entities?lat=12.97&lng=77.59&radius=5000&type=driver&limit=50
Response: {"entities": [...], "count": 42}

Security notes: location updates authenticated via device tokens. User location in queries is never logged with user_id (privacy). Rate-limit location updates to 1 per 3 seconds per entity to prevent abuse.

8. High-Level Design

FR1: Find nearby places (static entities)

Read the requirement plainly: given a point and a radius, return the places inside it. Places have a latitude and a longitude, so store those and query them.

Build that and nothing else. One service and one database. No spatial index, no cache, no second store for attributes — each of those answers a non-functional requirement, so each belongs in a deep dive where we can show why it is needed rather than asserting it here.

New components we need:

  1. Nearby Service - Takes a point and radius, finds the places inside it, returns them with their metadata.
  2. Place DB (Postgres) - One row per place: lat, lng, category, rating, opening hours. 200M rows, indexed on lat and lng.

Flow:

  1. User requests restaurants within 2km of their location
  2. The Nearby Service converts the radius into a degree box — 2km is about 0.018° of latitude — and queries WHERE lat BETWEEN ? AND ? AND lng BETWEEN ? AND ?
  3. The box is a square and the requirement is a circle, so every returned row gets an exact haversine distance and anything beyond 2km is dropped
  4. Sort the survivors by distance and return the nearest 20 with their metadata

Why a bounding box before the haversine, rather than haversine on everything? Because haversine involves trigonometry and cannot use an index — there is no way to ask a B-tree for “rows whose computed distance is under 2km”. The box is the part a database can actually narrow with an index, and the haversine then runs only on what survived. That instinct is right. The problem is how little the box actually narrows.

What we have deliberately left broken. This returns correct results, and three things about it are indefensible:

  • The bounding box barely narrows anything. A B-tree orders rows on one dimension, and proximity is two-dimensional. An index on lat gives a horizontal band that wraps the entire planet in longitude; within that band the database cannot also use lng efficiently, because a composite (lat, lng) index sorts by lat first. A 0.036° band over 200M places is roughly 40,000 rows read to return 20 — and places cluster in cities, so in a dense area it is far worse. That is Deep Dive 1.
  • Every request does this work from scratch. Two users standing in the same square get the same answer computed twice. In a city centre that is the same query running thousands of times a second. That is Deep Dive 3.
  • Step 4 sorts on distance alone. The nearest result is whatever is physically closest, which is not the same as what the user wants. That is Deep Dive 4.

FR2: Update location for moving entities

Drivers and friends move, so unlike a restaurant their position is a value that changes every few seconds. The requirement is that a query reflects a move within 3-5 seconds.

New components we need:

  1. Location Ingestion API - Accepts a GPS ping and records the entity’s current position.

The positions live in an entities table alongside the places table from FR1 — same database, same kind of query. A moving entity is a place whose row gets overwritten.

Flow:

  1. The driver app sends a GPS ping every 3-5 seconds
  2. The API returns 202 Accepted without waiting for anything downstream — the client has no decision to make based on the result, so making it wait buys nothing💡 HTTP 202 means “I have taken your request and have not finished acting on it”, as opposed to 200’s “done”. It is the honest status code for a fire-and-forget write like a GPS ping.
  3. It updates that entity’s row in place: new lat, lng, and a seen_at timestamp. One row per entity, overwritten, so the table does not grow with ping volume
  4. A nearby-entities query is the same bounding box as FR1, against this table instead

Why overwrite rather than append a position history? Because the requirement is “where is this driver now”, and nothing on this page asks where they were. One row per entity keeps the table at 10M rows instead of 10M rows a second, and the query stays the same shape as FR1’s.

Why does seen_at exist? This one is correctness rather than scale, which is why it belongs here. A driver whose app crashes or loses signal stops sending pings but their last position stays in the table forever, so they keep appearing in results as a ghost. Treat anything older than about 30 seconds as offline and exclude it.

What we have deliberately left broken. The write volume. 10M concurrent moving entities pinging every 4 seconds is 2.5M writes per second, and every one of them is an UPDATE to an indexed row, which means Postgres rewrites the row, updates both the lat and lng indexes, and writes it all to the write-ahead log (WAL).💡 The write-ahead log is the file a database appends every change to before the change counts as committed, and it is what makes a crash survivable. It also means one logical update costs several physical writes. Learn more → No single relational database does that, and no amount of read optimisation in Deep Dive 1 helps, because this is the write path. That is Deep Dive 2.

FR3: Search with filters (combined geo + attribute query)

“Nearby” is rarely the whole question. The real one is “Italian, open now, at least four stars, within 2km.”

New components we need: none, and that is worth dwelling on. The attributes are columns on the same rows FR1 already queries, so a filter is a WHERE clause on a query we are already running.

Flow:

  1. The request arrives with a point, a radius, and any mix of category, rating and open-now
  2. All of it goes into one SQL statement: the bounding box plus category = ?, rating >= ?, and an opening-hours predicate
  3. The survivors get the exact haversine distance and are sorted
  4. Return the top 20

Why is this the one requirement that gets easier at scale, not harder? Because the filters reduce the result set. The bounding box from FR1 reads ~40,000 rows; adding category = 'restaurant' AND rating >= 4 throws most of them away before any distance maths. Filtering is free work that makes the expensive part smaller.

What we have deliberately left broken. Nothing yet — and that is the interesting part, because this section is about to be broken by a fix rather than by a load.

Filters are cheap here for exactly one reason: geography and attributes live in the same rows of the same database, so one query can constrain both. Deep Dive 1 is about to move the geography into a dedicated spatial index to fix FR1’s 40,000-row scan, and the moment it does, that property is gone. The spatial index knows where things are and nothing about cuisine or rating; the database knows the attributes and cannot answer proximity quickly. A filtered nearby query then has to span two stores, and whichever one runs first hands the other a list it has to re-filter.

So the cost of Deep Dive 1 is paid here, and Deep Dive 1 has to say what replaces this.

9. Technology Choices

Tier Purpose Stores Access Pattern Primary Pick Alternatives
Spatial index (static) Index places and restaurants Place records with geohash Prefix range scan + radius filter Redis Geo / Elasticsearch geo_point PostGIS / DynamoDB with geohash sort key
Spatial index (dynamic) Real-time moving entities Driver or friend locations High-frequency updates + radius query Redis Geo (in-memory) Custom quadtree service
Place metadata Full place details Name, reviews, photos, hours Point lookup by place_id Postgres / DynamoDB MongoDB
Cache Hot query results Nearby results per geohash cell Key-value with short TTL Redis / Memcached CDN edge cache
Event stream Location update ingestion GPS pings from mobile devices Append-only high throughput Kafka / Kinesis Redis Streams
scroll →

Why Redis Geo for dynamic entities? Moving entities (drivers, friends) update every 3-5 seconds. Redis Geo gives O(log N) updates + O(N+log M) radius queries, all in memory. For 2M active drivers, this fits in ~1-2GB RAM and handles 500K updates/sec on a single shard. PostGIS would buckle under this write rate.

10. Data Modeling

Redis Geo (Spatial Index — static places and dynamic entities):

Key: "places:{city}:{category}" → Geo Set (member = placeId, lat/lng encoded as geohash score)
Key: "drivers:active:{city}" → Geo Set (member = driverId)
Key: "friends:live:{userId}" → Geo Set (member = friendId)

Postgres / DynamoDB (Place Metadata — full details):

CREATE TABLE places (
    place_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    category VARCHAR(50),   -- restaurant, cafe, gym, hospital
    lat DECIMAL(10,7) NOT NULL,
    lng DECIMAL(10,7) NOT NULL,
    geohash VARCHAR(12),    -- precomputed for bucketing
    rating DECIMAL(2,1),
    price_range INTEGER,    -- 1-4
    hours JSONB,            -- operating hours per day
    address TEXT,
    city VARCHAR(100)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_places_geohash ON places(geohash);
CREATE INDEX idx_places_city_cat ON places(city, category);
SQL

Redis (Query Result Cache):

Key: "nearby:{geohash6}:{category}:{radius}" → JSON list of place summaries
TTL: 60 seconds (short TTL since results are location-dependent)

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Find restaurants within 2km Redis Geo GEOSEARCH places:{city}:restaurant FROMLONLAT lng lat BYRADIUS 2 km COUNT 50 ASC
Filter by rating > 4.0 Application Post-filter Redis Geo results against Postgres metadata (or Elasticsearch for complex queries)
Update driver location Redis Geo GEOADD drivers:active:{city} lng lat driverId every 3-5s
Get place details Postgres SELECT * FROM places WHERE place_id = ?
scroll →

How the Nearest Driver Query Works with Redis Geo:

  1. Rider requests ride at (28.6139, 77.2090) → service calls GEOSEARCH drivers:active:delhi FROMLONLAT 77.2090 28.6139 BYRADIUS 3 km COUNT 20 ASC
  2. Redis internally: converts query point to geohash, does range scan on the sorted set score, computes Haversine distance for candidates in matching geohash cells
  3. Returns up to 20 drivers sorted by distance — entire operation takes ~0.5ms for 200K drivers in the set
  4. For filtered queries (e.g., “only Italian restaurants, open now, rating > 4”): use Elasticsearch with geo_distance filter + bool query on attributes — trades Redis speed for richer filtering

11. Deep Dives

1) A B-tree sorts on one dimension and proximity has two. What indexes a map?

Problem: FR1 narrows with a bounding box on lat and lng. That is the best a B-tree can do and it is not close to good enough, because the structure of the index does not match the shape of the question.

Bad: the bounding box FR1 built. The reason it fails is worth being precise about, because “add an index” is the instinct and the index already exists.

A B-tree is a sorted list. An index on lat can hand you every row in a latitude band, which is a strip wrapping the entire planet. An index on lng can hand you a strip wrapping it the other way. What you want is the intersection, and a B-tree cannot give you that — a composite (lat, lng) index sorts by lat first, so once it has your band it can only scan within it. Two one-dimensional indexes cannot answer a two-dimensional question.

The arithmetic: 2km is about 0.018° of latitude, so the box is a 0.036° band, which is 0.02% of the planet’s latitudes. Over 200M places that is roughly 40,000 rows fetched and haversine-d to return 20 — a 2,000:1 waste ratio. And that assumes places are spread evenly. They are not; they cluster in exactly the dense city centres where the query gets asked most, so the real figure in Manhattan or Bangalore is far higher. The P99 target is 100ms.

— interleave the bits of latitude and longitude into a single string, so that a shared prefix means spatial proximity. Now one sorted index answer the two-dimensional question: a prefix scan on returns the points in that cell, and the data structure can be anything that sorts — a Redis sorted set, a DynamoDB sort key, even a B-tree on a varchar column.

The catch is that the cells are a fixed grid of rectangles, and a circle is not a grid. Two points 50m apart can sit either side of a cell boundary and therefore share no prefix, so a correct query has to scan the centre cell and still filter by exact distance. Cell sizes also vary with latitude, because longitude degrees converge toward the poles.

(Uber) or (Google). H3 uses hexagons, which have uniform adjacency — every cell has exactly 6 neighbours, all equidistant, where a geohash rectangle has 8 at two different distances. That regularity is what removes the edge-case class above rather than just shrinking it. S2 instead maps the sphere onto a Hilbert curve, which gives better spatial locality in the 1D index than geohash’s Z-order curve, so a radius query touches fewer disjoint ranges.

Pick by precision requirement rather than by sophistication. For “restaurants near me”, geohash is sufficient and its ubiquity is worth more than H3’s uniformity. For ride matching, where a cell-boundary artefact means dispatching the second-nearest driver, H3 or S2 earns its complexity.

Moving geography into a dedicated spatial index splits it from the attributes, so a filtered nearby query now spans two stores and neither can answer it alone. Three options, and the right one depends on selectivity:

The practical answer is to route on query shape: unfiltered proximity goes to the spatial index, which is the fastest path; anything with filters goes to the store that can evaluate both at once. That routing is the real cost of this deep dive, and it is why FR3 was easy and will not stay that way.

2) 2.5M position writes a second, every one an indexed UPDATE. What gives out first?

Problem: FR2 updates a row per ping. Deep Dive 1 fixed the read path and made the write path worse, because a spatial index is one more index to maintain on every one of those writes.

Bad: the per-ping UPDATE from FR2. 10M concurrent entities pinging every 4 seconds is 2.5M writes per second, and a relational UPDATE to an indexed row is not one write. For each ping Postgres writes a new row version, updates the lat index, updates the lng index, appends to the write-ahead log, and leaves a dead tuple for vacuum to reclaim later.💡 Postgres never edits a row in place - it writes a new version and leaves the old one as garbage (a “dead tuple”) for a background process called vacuum to clear up. At this write rate vacuum cannot keep up, so the table bloats even though the number of drivers never grows. Call it a handful of disk operations per ping, so single-digit millions of pings becomes tens of millions of write operations a second against one primary.

Three distinct things break, and they are worth separating:

  • Throughput. This is one to two orders of magnitude past what a single Postgres primary sustains, and it cannot be sharded away cheaply because proximity queries need to span shards.
  • Index churn. Every position change rewrites index entries. The indexes that make FR1’s read tolerable are precisely what makes this write expensive — the two requirements are fighting over the same structure.
  • Vacuum. At 2.5M dead tuples a second, autovacuum falls behind permanently, tables bloat, and the reads get slower over time even though the row count never grows.

Note also what we are paying for: a driver sitting at a traffic light sends the same coordinate fifteen times, and we do all of that work fifteen times to store a value that did not change.

For each ping Postgres writes a new row version, updates the index, updates the index, appends to the write-ahead log, and leaves a dead tuple for vacuum to reclaim later. Call it a handful of disk operations per ping, so single-digit millions of pings becomes tens of millions of write operations a second against one primary.

Note also what we are paying for: a driver sitting at a traffic light sends the same coordinate fifteen times, and we do all of that work fifteen times to store a value that did not change.

Move positions to an in-memory store with a native geo type. Redis is O(log N) against a sorted set, there is no WAL fsync in the hot path and no vacuum, and a single shard handles a few hundred thousand ops a second — so shard by city or region and 2.5M/sec is reachable. This also collapses Deep Dive 1 and this dive into one answer, since the geo index and the position store become the same structure. The remaining problem is that we are still doing full work for the driver at the traffic light.

Not all entities need 3-second updates. A parked driver can report every 30 seconds. A driver mid-trip needs 3-second updates. The mobile SDK adapts based on movement speed (GPS delta < 5m → throttle). This alone reduces write volume by 60-70%. Combined with edge batching (agent on the device buffers 3-5 pings and sends one batch), actual write QPS to the spatial index drops to ~500K — well within Redis Geo capacity.

3) Why does a cache keyed on the user’s coordinates never get a single hit?

Problem: FR1 recomputes every query from scratch, and in a city centre thousands of people a second are asking a question with the same answer. Caching is obviously right, and the obvious cache key does not work.

Bad: FR1’s recompute-every-time, and then the obvious fix for it — cache on the request as it arrives, keyed (lat, lng, radius). The second is barely better than the first, because its hit rate is approximately zero.

A GPS fix carries about seven decimal places, which is centimetre resolution. Two people standing beside each other, or the same person holding still while the fix drifts, produce different keys. So every request is a miss, every miss does FR1’s 40,000-row scan, and we have added a network hop and a memory footprint to a system that gets no benefit whatsoever. Worse than useless: the cache fills with millions of single-use entries and evicts anything that might have been reused.

The insight is that the key has too much precision for the question. Nobody asking for restaurants within 2km needs an answer specific to their centimetre.

Round the request to its enclosing geohash cell — precision 6 is roughly 1.2km — and key the cache on the cell rather than the point. Everyone in that cell now shares one entry, so in a dense area the hit rate jumps to the 60-80% range. The cost is that someone at the edge of a cell gets results computed from the cell’s centre, which can be a few hundred metres off; acceptable for “nearby restaurants”, not for anything where the exact ordering of the first two results matters.

For the most popular cells (city centers, airport areas), proactively compute “nearby restaurants within 2km” every 30 seconds and push to the cache. These cells serve 80% of all queries, and users get sub-5ms responses without ever hitting the spatial index. Less popular cells fall back to on-demand caching.

4) The nearest restaurant is usually not the one you want. What should “nearby” sort by?

Problem: FR1 sorts by distance because distance is what it computed. That is the index’s preference showing up in the product, not an answer to what the user asked.

Bad: sort purely by distance, as FR1 does. The first result is a 1-star takeaway 50m away and the 4.8-star restaurant 300m away is fourth. Those 250 metres are about three minutes of walking — a difference no diner would trade a three-star rating gap for, and the system makes that trade on their behalf every time.

The failure gets worse as the data gets better. Add more places and the top of a distance-sorted list fills with whatever happens to be closest, so density actively degrades the first screen — which is the only part most users read. Distance is a constraint the user already expressed by choosing a radius; re-using it as the ranking signal answers a question they already answered.

Score on distance and rating together, for example . Two lines, immediately better, and tunable. Its limits are that the weights are guesses applied identically to everyone, and it only knows the two signals that happen to be columns — not price, not whether the place is open, not whether this user has ever liked anywhere similar.

that considers: distance, rating, number of reviews, price match to user preference, open-now status, click-through history for this user, and trending/popular-right-now signals. The model is trained on user engagement data (which results do users actually click and visit?). Served via a lightweight ML model (gradient boosted trees) that scores the top-100 spatial results and re-ranks to top-20. Latency budget: 10-20ms for re-ranking after the spatial query returns.

12. Design Self-Audit

  • Stale reads? Dynamic entity positions lag by 3-5 seconds (GPS ping interval). Acceptable for “nearby friends” but tight for ride matching (Uber uses <1 second with WebSocket push).
  • Single points of failure? Redis Geo is sharded by city and replicated. Kafka provides durability for the location update stream. Place metadata in Postgres with read replicas.
  • Dead-letter / reconciliation? If Redis Geo loses data (failover), replay the last 60 seconds from Kafka to rebuild state.💡 Kafka is a durable log of events that consumers read at their own pace and can re-read from any point. That replayability is what turns “the in-memory index was wiped” from an incident into a sixty-second catch-up. Learn more →
  • Hot partition? Manhattan/CBD areas have 100x the density of suburbs. Shard spatial index by geohash prefix regions, with hot regions getting more replicas.💡 Here the hot partition is geographic: splitting the world into equal-sized cells does not split the traffic equally, because people and queries cluster in city centres. The shard holding Manhattan does far more work than the one holding farmland. Learn more →
  • Cost? Redis in-memory is expensive at scale. 10M entities x ~100 bytes = ~1GB — very affordable. The cost is dominated by Location Ingestion API compute (handling 2M pings/sec), not storage.

13. Core Flows

Flow 1: Nearby Query

Non-obvious failure path: If the spatial index is temporarily unavailable, return stale cached results (degrade gracefully). Cache keys include the geohash cell (not exact lat/lng) so nearby users hit the same cache entry, improving hit rate.

14. Final Architecture

How it works end-to-end:

  1. User searches for nearby places — request hits Load Balancer, routed to Nearby Service
  2. Result Cache checked — Redis returns cached results for repeated queries (same geohash cell)
  3. Static index queried — Elasticsearch geo_point index returns fixed locations (restaurants, gas stations) within radius
  4. Dynamic index queried — Redis Geo shards return live-moving entities (drivers, riders) near the user
  5. Results merged and returned — Nearby Service combines static + dynamic results, ranked by distance/relevance
  6. Drivers update location — Driver App sends GPS pings to Location Ingestion service
  7. Kafka streams updates — location events published for async processing
  8. Index Updater refreshes Redis Geo — consumes from Kafka and writes latest positions to the sharded dynamic spatial index
